## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Engineers at AI-native startups keeping an LLM agent working for customers in production.
   [LYC] "Before starting Lemma, we were engineers at two high growth, AI-native startups: Tandem (AI for healthcare) and
   Chipstack (AI agents for chip design)." [LYC] "If you're building with LLMs and run a ton of prompt or eval
   experiments, we'd love for you to work with us." → `roles[engineer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep the agent doing what customers need as real traffic changes.
   [LYC] "AI agents don't learn from their mistakes. In fact, they get worse with use." [LYC] "In production, prompts
   and agents continuously degrade due to real-world input drift (new user behaviors or unseen edge cases)."
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When the agent starts failing on real inputs nobody tested.
   [LYC] "Agent performance can often drop ~40% in a few weeks, and suddenly what worked in testing breaks in front of
   customers." [LYC] "When that happens, engineers are forced to dig through logs, collect failing examples, and manually
   tweak prompts rather than building core product features." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: agent failure`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; the launch says
   "continuously" and gives no count. The daily rhythm is confirmed only later, by a customer quote on [SITE]: "Every
   morning, I check our frontend logs -> backend logs -> Lemma logs, then pipe any issues straight into Claude".
   Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most") is the author's: not every team's agent fails every week.

4. **Which people.** Engineers at US pre-seed to Series A startups with an agent serving customers.
   [LYC] "If you know a Head of AI/Eng or CTO at a pre-seed to Series A startup, we owe you lunch :)" → `context.segment`,
   `market: US` (author's choice: the founders are in the US batch and name no other market).

5. **Who pays.** The startup; its CTO or head of AI decides.
   [LYC] the ask above names the buyer, no payer or terms. → `persona.decision_maker: {role: founder}` (label
   "Startup CTOs and founders"; the id reads "The founder decides" in the engine's sentence). Buyer and payer tests
   "Nobody else" (at pre-seed the technical founder buys tools alone), with "The CEO" and "The security lead" listed:
   author's choice. Purchase friction's three items (a security review of sending traces out — tested; a check against
   the current observability tool; access to open pull requests) are the author's, drawn from [LYC]'s mechanism
   ("automatically open a PR in your codebase") and [YCP]'s "the silent failures your observability tools and evals
   miss". Commitment's step "connect one agent's traces for a trial": [LYC] "book a live demo on our website"; [WB]
   "Book a demo appointment to get started."; the trial on one agent is the author's next step after the demo.

6. **Mechanism.** Failed runs found in live traffic; the cause traced; a prompt fix opened as a pull request.
   [LYC] "Step 1: Lemma detects failed outcomes directly from live traffic, and it automatically identifies the exact
   cause in an agent chain." "Step 2: Lemma alerts you, and with one click, it runs targeted prompt optimizations to fix
   the failing behavior without any manual tracing or guesswork." "Step 3: We give you back an improved prompt and
   automatically open a PR in your codebase so your prompts can live where you want them." [LYC] "Agent tracing
   observability with live drift detection, regression alerts, and performance visibility across real user
   interactions." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (every run already traced — tested;
   prompts in the repository; traces may leave the company) and Adoption friction (review and merge the prompt changes
   it opens — tested; add its tracing to the agent's code). Relative advantage: [LYC] "resolve production drifts in
   minutes instead of days" (easier_recovery) and "cut manual prompt iteration by 90%" (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or since; the cost is a rate of failing runs.
   [LYC] asks for demos and introductions and names no price; [WB] "Book a demo appointment to get started."; [PRC] 404.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $300 to $600 per agent a month: **the operator's reading**, not a source. The
   unit is the cost's (a chain price follows the cost's unit and period); the amount is the author's, a sum a CTO can
   approve alone that sits well under one engineer-week ([BLS]). `statements.commercial` carries the same reading.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 10% to 40% of the agent's runs in production per agent a month, lossPhrase "Runs that fail in
   front of customers before anyone notices": the top is [LYC]'s "~40%", read as a share of runs (the launch says
   "performance"); the low end is the author's. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent of runs never
   compares with dollars), so the six founders answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "dig through logs, collect failing examples, and manually tweak prompts". [YCP] "We catch the silent failures
   your observability tools and evals miss (think bad tool calls, lost context, and infinite loops) before your users
   find them." (today's page, later than launch). [SITE] (customer, later) "almost immediately it flagged an issue that
   had gone unnoticed in prod for 20+ days".

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

AI engineers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priya Venkataraman → [LYC] "what worked in testing breaks in front of customers"; the refund window from [SITE]'s demo incident ("P0 — promising refunds outside 30-day policy", later); the rest the author's.
- Mateo Fernández → [YCP] "infinite loops" and "bad tool calls" (later page); the bill spike the author's.
- Aisha Bello → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose own eval suite catches regressions before they ship (against on Importance), so the problem is not a chorus.
- Jonah Feldman → [LYC] "collect failing examples, and manually tweak prompts"; [YCP] "lost context".
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Kwabena Asare → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED; Frequency `cant_recall`).
- Sofia Marchetti → author's invention: a gate No (her team's agent not yet live that week).
- Ravi Shankar → author's invention: a gate No (on leave).
- Daniel Kim → [SITE]'s demo failure mode ("the agent invents placeholder identifiers instead of asking"; "Every one returned success, so nothing surfaced in error monitoring.", later); he will not merge machine-written prompt changes (Adoption friction probably not).
- Elena Petrova → [LYC] the founders' healthcare background (Tandem); author's invention: runs only sampled and patient details stripped, so the tested condition fails for her (Compatibility only with help).
- Tyrone Jackson → author's invention, filling a gap: latency and cost, not wrong answers, are his week's problem (against on Importance).
- Hannah Goldberg → [LYC] "new user behaviors or unseen edge cases"; the language mix-up the author's.
- Omar Haddad → [P2] "many existing agent monitoring systems depend heavily on developers deciding beforehand what they want to measure. This can include configuring specific judges, traces, evaluation criteria, alerts or known failure conditions." — a team whose own judges catch the known failures (Current solution mostly works).
- Lucía Romero → [LYC] the manual prompt loop; [SITE]'s "Agents can look like they're working even when they've failed." (later).

Startup CTOs and founders (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Nathan Cole → [LYC] the ask to "a Head of AI/Eng or CTO at a pre-seed to Series A startup"; pays below the founder's band per agent (several small agents; the per-agent price adds up), though he would start the trial.
- Farah Siddiqui → author's invention: prices it below the band against the observability tool she already pays for, and wants a week on staging first (Commitment yes after trying).
- Wei Zhang → [SITE] (customer, later) "we switched over from raindrop a while back": a buyer who already pays for an observability tool and prices this below it.
- Isabel Duarte → [SITE] (customer, later) "it flagged an issue that had gone unnoticed in prod for 20+ days": a buyer who would pay above the band (beyond), with the CEO agreeing.
- Marcus Oyelaran → author's invention, filling a gap: a low-volume agent read by hand, so Nothing as the cost and would not pay.
- Chloe Bennett → [P2] agents "in workflows where failures have financial, operational or customer-facing consequences"; author's invention: a security lead who must clear any vendor seeing customer conversations, and a buyer who cannot say the cost or the price (both escapes).

The split (1 of the 5 founders who name a rung at $300 or above, the other four below it -- made harsher on
2026-10-22 so the price fails; 3 of 5 cost boxes at 10% or more) is the author's
reading of a crowded tooling market ([P2] "The emerging AI observability market includes tools for tracing model calls,
measuring latency, monitoring token usage, evaluating model responses and reviewing agent behavior.") against the
launch's claims. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, re-led. The problem is unchanged (agents fail in production without anyone noticing); the lead product moved
from "Continuous Learning" and automated prompt optimization ([LYC], [WB]) to monitoring: [SITE] "Lemma | Production
monitoring for AI agents"; "Lemma audits every trace against your agent's instructions and groups recurring failures
into issues."; "Pull context into your coding agent to resolve it without context-switching." Raised $2.3 million
pre-seed ([P2], 2026-08-19). Price today: none public ([PRC] 404; [SITE] "Book a demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price, at any time.** The founder's $300 to $600 per agent a month is the operator's reading (item 7), recorded
  as such in the entry's header and in `statements.commercial`. A run that reads the price line reads the author's
  number, not Lemma's.
- **A share of runs.** [LYC]'s 40 is a fall in "performance", not a share of failing runs; the RATE reading and its low
  end of 10 are the author's (header).
- **A buyer title in practice, the approvers and the purchase steps.** Only the launch ask names the buyer; the CEO and
  security lead, the three Purchase friction items and the trial step are the author's.
- **An engineer's hour.** [BLS]'s software developers' median stands in; a RATE cost does not use it.
- **The daily rhythm at launch.** The launch says "continuously"; the morning-check quote is today's site.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person engineer accounts from the launch era.** None found; the customer quotes on
  [SITE] are vendor-curated and later than launch.

insights_note: no grouping to read (no follow-up line with two answers)

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to sending, but the window question (screen 4) sits between two screens with the identical context heading, so the context step feels split around it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 both ask 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks about my solution (finding failed runs in live traffic, tracing the cause, opening a prompt-fix PR) or the commercial side. There is no question on who decides and pays (the CTO or head of AI at a pre-seed to Series A startup), what it costs today in failing runs, or a price per agent. There is also no question on whether teams already trace every run or would let traces leave the company, which my product depends on.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 3 asks me to pick what I'd most like made easier before screen 4 asks how my last failure actually went, so I'm choosing a wish before I've recalled the concrete incident that would inform it.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 1 and 2 overlap -- screen 2's count of failing days already answers screen 1's yes/no.
PRIMARY.missing: What the failure actually was (e.g. a policy violation like promising refunds outside the 30-day window, a bad tool call, a loop), how I found out about it (customer report, alert, eval), how long it took to fix, and whether I added the failing input back into my test set.

screens.why2: "What should we call this project?" is plain to any founder on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my company's name and tagline; nothing here asks me to guess.

screens.why3: I know my respondents, mostly engineers who'd rather tap through text between deploys than sit on a video call, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: AI voice, text only, or offer both covers every real choice without overlap, and the readiness notes ('Ready now', 'ready in a few minutes') tell me what each costs me in waiting.
screens.why5: Nothing about Lemma, prompts or PRs leaks into the format choice, and 'AI engineers' is still my word for the people I'm asking.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how engineers answer, deciding who receives a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Short, plain options I read once; 'link', 'Contacts page' and 'sign in with Google' are everyday words to a founder who ships software.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm emailing engineers I know from Tandem and Chipstack circles, pulling a list, or posting in a Slack or Discord where AI engineers hang out.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the option labels run straight into their descriptions with no separator, and 'People I found with Keel' leans on a Contacts page I haven't seen in this flow.
screens.why5: Nothing of my problem or product is restated here, so nothing drifts, and my pick of named people is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / A list from Keel's Contacts search (Keel makes a link per person; I send them) / A group I post one open link to (each person signs in with Google first)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it ('Frequency: 4 answered', and the card says 5 were needed), so I know the problem stage is not called yet and why.
screens.why_b2: The tally '1 holding · 3 too few · 7 people answered' and each card's 'n answered · bar' are plain, but I needed a second look to see why only 4 of the 7 count on three cards when 6 of 7 said yes on Prevalence; nothing says where the other two or three went.
screens.why_b3: The four card names and belief lines are the ones I checked, including 'Shipping new features on schedule is one of the two' for Importance and 'digging through logs and tweaking prompts by hand' for Current solution.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do with three of four problem beliefs uncalled; the only footer is 'What it measures', with no line saying to reach more engineers, or how many more, before I read Importance or Current solution as an answer.
screens.why_b5: Prevalence is scoped 'among these 7' with 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, the three thin cards are called too few rather than leaning either way, and n is visible everywhere.
screens.instead: Not called yet: only 4 of the 7 engineers who answered could be counted on Frequency, Importance and Current solution (5 needed), so send the study to a few more engineers whose agent is live before reading whether the hand-fixing loop really falls short; Prevalence already holds, 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up above your band' sits directly over '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against on a 0 to 7 axis with the marker at 5 labelled 'your bar · 5 of 7 (at least 6 in 10)', so what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits are clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: It names my actor and my circumstance almost word for word ('agent in production start failing on real inputs', 'last 5 working days'), though the band reads '6 to 7 in 10' where I meant most, and the bar label says 'at least 6 in 10'.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' and a pointer to the next two cards tell me where to look, but not what this means for Lemma, such as that failures are frequent enough to build on, so the case rests on how often they happen and what they cost.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' tempers 'above your band'; counting Sofia's gate No against me is conservative, not flattering.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 had their production agent fail on real inputs this week, so the failure is common, not rare; with only 7 this is a lean, and whether Lemma is worth buying turns on the Frequency and Importance cards next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed', but the count line says 6 answered and 4 counted, and the bar line's '3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)' reads like a pass, so the deciding number is muddled.
screens.why_b2: Working days out of 5, 3 of 4 counted and the marker at 3 are all on the chart, but the legend's 'what you said at what you said short of it' needs a second look to parse.
screens.why_b3: Frequency and '3 to 5 working days out of 5' for an agent failing on real inputs is exactly the window and rhythm I set.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it never says that one more engineer with a clear, recent count would settle it, or that 3 of 4 lean my way.
screens.why_b5: It names the small group as a lean, not a call, keeps n visible and shows who was dropped and why, so nothing is overclaimed.
screens.instead: 6 answered, 4 counted (Mei-Ling declined, Kwabena guessed); 3 of 4 put failures on 3 to 5 days, which leans your way, but one more counted answer is needed to call it, so get one more engineer to name last week's days.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats it.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes clear the bars count 8 picks from 4 people and the bar is 3 of 4. But the strip under it shows 3 for and 5 against, 8 cells for 4 people, so I had to look twice to see it was counting picks, not people (only Aisha is against).
screens.why_b3: Importance and 'Shipping new features on schedule is one of the two they would most like made easier' are word for word the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' tells me not to act, but not what to do. It should say one more counted answer would settle it, and that 3 of 4 already sits over my bar of 2 in 3.
screens.why_b5: n and the small group are said plainly. But the strip's 'against 5' reads as five people against when only one is, and the verdict's '4 answered' clashes with the count line's '6 answered · 4 counted'.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 6 counted, 5 needed. 3 of the 4 put shipping features in their two (only Aisha didn't), so one more counted engineer settles it; ask Mei-Ling or Kwabena again, or send it to one more.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats '4 counted, 5 needed', so I know why there is no call yet.
screens.why_b2: The chart shows what is counted (where each engineer's last failure landed against my line) over 4 people, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' sits where a result would and reads like one, though all 4 counted are for me, and the ghost fifth cell takes a second look to read as the missing answer.
screens.why_b3: The card's title and belief line match what I checked word for word: digging through logs and tweaking prompts by hand still falls short.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't say that one more counted answer would settle it, or that every counted answer so far is below my line.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said plainly ('a lean, not a call'), but the verdict's '4 answered' contradicts the count line's '6 answered', and Aisha's 'evals caught it, fixed within the day' is counted as my way falling short when her own evals worked, which flatters my belief.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 6 counted and all 4 fell short of an alert-and-fast-fix, though one was caught by the team's own evals within the day. One more counted answer would settle it, so ask two more engineers about their last failure.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', but the screen never says how many of the 4 put features in their two, so I cannot see how close the belief came.
screens.why_b3: The Importance name and the belief line are word for word the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next: whether to send the study to more engineers, or how many more to reach a call.
screens.why_b5: One quote is shown as one ('On their own (1)', '1 against · 1 asked their why here'), and nothing is claimed beyond the four who answered.
screens.why_b6: Aisha's line adds that an eval suite can catch regressions before they ship, and that latency competes with features; the trailing 'Keeping model and inference costs down, Hiring enough engineers' list sits unlabelled, so I cannot tell if it is her two or the field.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 put shipping features in their two, 1 more answer needed; the one against (Aisha) says her eval suite already catches regressions, so speed and cost slip instead. Send to at least one more engineer.

screens.why1: As the first gate screen, it obviously makes sense to check whether my agent actually broke on customer traffic recently before asking for the story.
screens.why2: "Start failing" makes me pause, because my agent gets something wrong every day, so I can't tell if this means a new regression or any bad output on a real customer conversation.
screens.why3: I watch our traces and support escalations every day, so I know straight away whether it went wrong on live traffic this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No are right, but a gate shouldn't carry escape chips at all, "I'd rather not say" isn't an allowed escape, and "I can't recall one particular production failure" doesn't fit a yes-or-no about the whole week.
screens.why5: It drops "that never came up in testing", which is the actual pain (what passed our evals breaks with customers), and keeps "real inputs", which reads like someone else's phrasing rather than mine.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question ending in "Yes or no", easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did your agent get something wrong with a customer that your testing never caught? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, asking how often it happened that week is the obvious next thing, and it doesn't repeat the first question.
screens.why2: "Start failing" counted by days reads oddly, because a bad prompt path or tool-call bug that starts on Monday is still failing on Tuesday, so I'd stop and wonder whether to count new breakages or every day it was broken.
screens.why3: I live in our traces and alerts, so I know which days last week we had customer-facing failures on inputs we never tested.
screens.why4: 1 to 5 covers every answer after a yes, with no overlap, and "I can't recall" fits a count question.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's own situation, an agent in production failing on real inputs, in words my trade uses, and nothing about a product leaks.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short question with "a number from 1 to 5" and a single escape, so it is easy to answer out loud.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did your agent in production fail on real inputs? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often my agent broke on real inputs, asking what I'd most want made easier last week is the natural next step.
screens.why2: Inference costs, latency for users, hiring and shipping on schedule are all words I use every day, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I live all of these every week, so I can pick from what actually happened rather than guess.
screens.why4: The thing that ate my week, catching and fixing the agent when it breaks on real customer inputs it never saw in testing, isn't on the list, so my true answer is missing and I'm pushed to 'None of these'.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the list has drifted from the study's own subject, the agent failing on real traffic, which the first two screens asked about and this one leaves out.
screens.why6: One short question and four parallel options I can hold by ear, with a single escape said last.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of keeping the agent running. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Catching the agent failing on real inputs · Keeping model and inference costs down · Keeping the agent fast enough for users · Shipping new features on schedule · or None of these

screens.why1: After asking what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last production failure actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The stem asks how digging through logs went, but half the options say it never came to logs, so I have to reread to see it is really asking how the failure was found and fixed.
screens.why3: I live this every week, so I can answer it straight from my last incident.
screens.why4: The options mix how it was caught with how fast it was fixed, so a customer report I then dug out of logs fits two rows, and the escape 'Someone else did it' is odd for a failure I own.
screens.why5: The stem presumes digging through logs as the way it went, which leans on the founder's own picture rather than my words.
screens.why6: It says once fairly well, but the five options are uneven mouthfuls that mix catching and fixing, and the swap to 'you' in 'you fixed it fast' sits oddly beside 'found it digging through logs'.
screens.instead: Think of your last production failure. How did you first find out about it? An alert; our evals; digging through logs; a customer told us; or we never found the cause. Or say I can't recall.
